subject: MSA/Order Form — framing aggregate vs per-year liability ceiling

Subject: Initial MSA redlines — liability ceiling framing

Jordan / Sarah,

Thanks again for the productive demo last week. I attached our latest MSA + Order Form redlines (see attach) — the primary open legal item is the limitation of liability section. To keep things actionable, I want to propose a narrow framing and two concrete options you can take back to your legal team:

- Framing: Redwood proposes a single aggregate monetary ceiling tied to fees paid in the prior 12 months (rolling 12). This aligns incentives for properly sized purchases and avoids over-indexing on a single long tail incident.

- Option A (preferred by Redwood): Aggregate annual cap = greater of (1x) 1x annual fees OR $500k; consequential damages excluded as standard, carveouts remain for IP breach, gross negligence, and third-party indemnities.
- Option B (fallback): Contract term cap = 3x total fees paid during contract term (useful when customers prefer a simple multiplier rather than rolling windows).

Quick asks: please let us know which option TideScale prefers and whether your legal team needs a per-incident cap in addition to the aggregate ceiling. If you push back on carveouts (IP/confidentiality), flag that too and we can escalate legal-to-legal.

Attachments: TideScale_MSA_redlines_20261018.pdf, OrderForm_TideScale_v3.xlsx

Best,
Jonas

Jonas,

Thanks for the clear options — helpful. Our GC (copied) is concerned about the $500k floor in Option A because our anticipated spend in year one will be modest (pilot customers). They asked whether we can remove the hard floor or scale it down to $100k for pilots.

Separately, they prefer an aggregate cap tied to total fees over the contract term (they find rolling 12 windows operationally messy). Their preliminary asks:

- Cap = 5x fees paid during the contract term OR $1M, whichever is greater.
- Keep carveouts for IP (we disagree on the scope here) and also an explicit exception for breaches of data protection obligations (they want these excluded from caps).

Are you able to push on the 5x and floor? Also, is Redwood open to a tiered approach where pilot year uses a lower floor?

Jordan

From: Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.inference>

Jonas — quick read and recommended stance below. High-level: we should aim to protect our economic exposure while remaining reasonable for pilots.

Recommended negotiating posture (Legal):
1) Keep monetary ceiling linked to fees, but accept customer's preference for term-based multiplier if it simplifies procurement — propose 2x total fees as our baseline (not 3x or 5x). This is defensible and consistent with market.

2) Remove the $500k hard floor for customers with confirmed pilot spend under $200k; instead add a sliding-floor: min($100k, 0.5x annual fees). For production deployments, maintain $500k floor or 1x annual fees floor (whichever is greater).

3) Data protection breaches: we cannot agree to unlimited exposure for data breaches. Counter-propose: data-protection breach carveout limited to amounts awarded by a final court judgment (no punitive/extra-contractual damages), capped at available insurance limits and subject to good-faith mitigation. This gives the customer some protection while keeping our exposure bounded.

4) Carveouts: keep IP and confidentiality carveouts narrow (will not include broad consequential claims). We can add a mutuality statement for IP breaches tied to willful infringement.

5) Per-incident caps: we accept a separate per-incident cap set at 0.5x annual fees to prevent single event outsized risk, with an aggregate cap at 2x term fees.

Escalation: if customer insists on 5x / unlimited data carveout, we need approval from Head of Legal + CRO for commercial offset (credits/price uplift). Karthik — please quantify the revenue delta for concessions vs. price adjustments so we can propose trade-offs.

I'll prepare redline text for option 2 and a clean comparison table you can send back.

- Laura

Subject: Re: Initial MSA redlines — liability ceiling framing

Jordan / Sarah — thanks for the quick return and helpful color. Our legal team dug in and asked me to propose a middle path that should address your GC's procurement concerns while keeping exposure reasonable for both parties. Summary below and attached redline:

- Redwood counter-proposal (commercial/legal compromise):
  • Aggregate cap = greater of (2x total fees paid during the contract term) OR $100k for pilot-year customers; for production customers the floor increases to $500k or 1x annual fees (whichever is greater).
  • Per-incident cap = 0.5x annual fees.
  • Data protection breaches: carveout limited to objectively awarded direct damages from a final judgment, recoverable up to available insurance limits; not unlimited.
  • IP/confidentiality carveouts preserved but scoped to willful misconduct / proven misappropriation rather than broad consequential categories.

If that structure is acceptable in principle we can produce a clean MSA/Order Form and route for procurement review. If TideScale's legal team still needs a 5x multiplier or an unlimited data carveout, please indicate that so we can surface the ask internally for pricing/credit trade-offs.

Attached: redline with the exact text we propose.

Best,
Jonas

Jonas/Laura,

Appreciate the detailed counter. The structure is promising — particularly the pilot-year floor accommodation and the split between per-incident and aggregate caps. Our GC will take this back and has asked for the precise redline text (the attached PDF you sent is fine). Two quick asks before we move to signatures:

1) Can you confirm whether the per-incident cap applies to a single claim regardless of number of plaintiffs (we prefer per-event language).
2) Provide a short explanation (1–2 paragraphs) on why the data protection carveout is limited to court-awarded damages vs. unlimited — our security team will escalate if they don't understand the rationale.

If those two clarifications are okay, we expect a clean sign-off next week and will begin procurement/PO flow.

Thanks — Sarah
